name: Priya Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm foreperson on a five-person crew out of the depot at Hollin Cross, which covers a big hilly farming district, so most of our lines run along hedges and across fields. I'm in at six, I check the job sheets, and by seven we're in the trucks heading out to a pole change or a fault from the night before. The bit I love is a clean job, everyone knowing where to stand without me saying it. The bit that wears me out is the paperwork, and now the company's new app that keeps popping up suggestions I never asked for.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's meant to plan our routes and write the job notes with some kind of AI helper. I don't touch it. Kofi, my apprentice, reads it out to me in the truck and I tell him what's actually going on at the site, because the app has never stood in a muddy field in February. I'm also the union rep for the depot, so I've already had words about it with management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. At the union meeting I'd say the bosses spent a fortune on gadgets and we still had to send a person up the pole. Online I don't say much, my sister does all that for the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job and my crew keeps theirs, and that's what I care about. I'd be relieved, though I'd still be cross about the money they wasted on that app instead of hiring two more linemen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes. I'd keep running the crew the way I do, keep pushing at the union for proper staffing on the winter rota, and keep paying a bit extra off the mortgage when the overtime comes in. Kofi would still read me the app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest with you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the money that went into the app have bought, if you'd had a say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two more linemen and a second bucket truck for the north end. Last January Dev and I did a sixteen-hour shift because there was nobody else, and I drove home with my hands shaking on the wheel. That's what I'd have spent it on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you be relieved for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, mostly. He's twenty and he's just started, and he's good, he's careful. I'd be glad he's got forty years of this ahead of him like I was told I had.

S0.say: I'd tell the union meeting that the bosses spent a fortune on gadgets and still had to send a person up the pole. I'd say I told you so.
S0.think: I'd be relieved that my crew keeps its work. I'd still be angry the money went on an app instead of two more linemen for the winter.
S0.do: Keeps running the crew the same way and keeps pressing the union for better winter staffing. Puts overtime money towards the mortgage as she already does.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug, with leftover anger about wasted money.
S0.quote: Kofi would still read me the app.
S0.fieldNote: Priya doesn't touch the AI tool at all and uses her apprentice to read it to her, which says a lot about how she handles new technology. Her anger points at management spending, not at the technology itself. The sixteen-hour shift story came out quickly and felt like a sore point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at the depot straight away: we need a deal in writing before any of it comes in. No job losses, retraining paid for by the company, and the crew gets a say. I'd say it at every meeting until people were sick of hearing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think they'd go after the inspections first. Drones already fly the lines in some areas, and the robot arms for live work are getting better. My hands are safe for a while, but the crew might shrink from five to four, and I don't want to be the one choosing who goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd get the regional union to ask for a technology agreement, so nothing new comes in without talks. I'd start putting an extra hundred a month into savings, which means the kids' summer camp gets shorter. I wouldn't go on any AI course, though, I'd leave that to Kofi.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like hearing thunder a long way off when you're up a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd leave the AI course to Kofi. What if the company made it part of your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go, and I'd sit at the back with my arms folded. I've done every safety course they've ever put in front of me. But I'd be counting the days until I'm back in the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila asked me last month if robots would take my job, because they talked about it at school. I told her robots can't climb in the rain like Mum can. I'm not sure I'd say it so confidently in this picture.

S1.say: I'd say we need a written deal before any of it comes in: no job losses, company-paid retraining and a say for the crew. I'd say it at every meeting.
S1.think: I think inspections go first and the crew shrinks from five to four. My own hands are safe for a while, but I don't want to be the one choosing who goes.
S1.do: Pushes the regional union for a technology agreement in the first month. Saves an extra hundred a month by cutting the kids' summer camp short, and avoids AI courses unless they're required.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like distant thunder while she's up a pole.
S1.quote: The crew might shrink from five to four, and I don't want to be the one choosing who goes.
S1.fieldNote: As foreperson, her worry is about having to choose who loses their job, more than about losing her own. She'd only do training if forced, and says so openly. The moment with her daughter Leila showed that her confidence is softer than her public line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what the union has been warning about, and the government has to step in now, not after. I'd want a pause on robots on the network until there's a plan for the people. I'd probably go to a protest, which I've only done twice in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be finished in this job inside two years, and I'd have nothing lined up. I'm not someone who picks up new things quickly, everyone at the depot knows it. We've got about three months of bills saved, and the mortgage has nineteen years left on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cut everything we can: the second car goes, Samir's football subscription, the holiday. I'd ask my brother whether we could move in with him if it came to it. And I'd be at every union meeting pushing for redundancy pay that actually covers a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the first time I saw a pole snap in a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What happens in the first few months while it's coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think I'd sleep. I'd be watching the depot notice board for the letter. I'd keep going up the poles every day, because I'd want every last shift of overtime in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people at the top who decide to buy robots instead of keeping people on. It's not the machines' fault. It's a choice, and it'll be made in an office far away from Hollin Cross.

S2.say: I'd say this is what the union warned about and the government must step in now. I'd call for a pause on robots on the network and probably join a protest.
S2.think: I think I'd be finished in the job inside two years with nothing lined up. I'm slow with new things, we have three months saved and nineteen years of mortgage.
S2.do: Cuts spending at once by selling the second car and dropping the holiday. Asks her brother about moving in if needed, and works every overtime shift while pushing the union for proper redundancy pay.
S2.feel: Sick to her stomach, losing sleep, like watching a pole snap in a storm.
S2.quote: It's a choice, and it'll be made in an office far away from Hollin Cross.
S2.fieldNote: Here her calm cracks completely: she can't see herself retraining in time and the savings won't stretch. She blames the decision-makers, not the technology, which fits her union outlook. Asking her brother for a place to live came up early, before I asked about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for the company or the government to be caught out. I'd say we want a law that a robot on the network means a person is kept on to look after it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two, but I'm not sure it's different for me. I'd be forty-eight and still not good with computers. What it gives me is time to get the mortgage down and get the kids a bit older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd overpay the mortgage every month, maybe two hundred extra, and stop the kitchen we were planning. I'd go to the union's national conference for the first time and argue for job guarantees for older linemen. I'd write to our local representative too, though Samir would have to type it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more like I'm doing something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the crew in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev would retire, he's sixty-one already, so that's one place that wouldn't need cutting. Kofi worries me most, because he'd only just be qualified when it lands. I'd tell him to get every ticket he can, even the computer ones I won't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's an interesting gap: you'd tell Kofi to do the computer training but you wouldn't. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because he's twenty and I'm forty-three, and you can laugh but I know my own head. I learned this trade by doing it with my hands for twenty years. I'd rather spend my energy fighting for a deal than sitting in a classroom failing.

S3.say: I'd say five years leaves no excuse for being caught out. I'd want a law that a robot on the network keeps a person employed to look after it.
S3.think: I think five years helps with the mortgage and the kids' ages more than with my skills. I'd be forty-eight and still not good with computers.
S3.do: Overpays the mortgage by about two hundred a month and drops the kitchen plans. Goes to the union's national conference to argue for job guarantees, and writes to the local representative.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadier because she'd be acting.
S3.quote: Kofi worries me most, because he'd only just be qualified when it lands.
S3.fieldNote: She sees the extra years as time for money and family, not for retraining herself, and she's frank about that. She pushes her apprentice to do the training she refuses. Her plan is to fight together with others rather than change on her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so let's see them do it properly. Shorter weeks, keep people on, share the savings. I'd say it on the union page and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years still lands me at fifty-three with Omar about to start college. I'd hope I could hold on until then. But I wouldn't bet the house on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the crew going, keep overpaying the mortgage, and keep pushing for a deal. I'd tell the kids to look at jobs where people need people, like nursing or teaching. I wouldn't change jobs myself, I'd fight to keep this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. There's room to breathe but it's still coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If someone offered you a different job in year three, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I know what I'm good at. I'd have to see the robots actually working in sleet before I'd walk away from twenty years of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Omar about his future, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to do something where you look people in the eye. He loves animals, so maybe a vet nurse. Not the lines, though, and that breaks my heart a little.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do it properly: shorter weeks, keeping people on, sharing the savings. I'd post it on the union page.
S4.think: I think ten years still leaves me at fifty-three with a son starting college. I'd hope to hold on, but I wouldn't bet the house on it.
S4.do: Keeps running the crew and overpaying the mortgage while pushing for a union deal. Steers the children towards caring jobs instead of the lines.
S4.feel: Uneasy but able to breathe, with some sadness about not passing on the trade.
S4.quote: Not the lines, though, and that breaks my heart a little.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years gives her enough room to feel uneasy rather than alarmed, mostly because it lines up with her children growing up. She still wouldn't move jobs herself and wants to see robots work in bad weather first. Steering her son away from the trade was the most emotional moment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is redundancy pay that covers the mortgage, and a rule that companies can't swap people for robots without a deal with the union first. Help with the mortgage for a year would mean we don't lose the house while I work out what's next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the weather. Every robot I've seen works on a sunny afternoon. Come out with us at three in the morning in an ice storm, and then tell me who's doing this job in 2028.

headlineQuote: Every robot I've seen works on a sunny afternoon.
portrait: Priya Ibrahim is a 43-year-old lineworker who runs a five-person crew in a hilly farming district and is the depot's union rep. She never touches AI tools and gets her apprentice to read the company app to her. She is calm about a plateau and uneasy about steady change, mostly because she might have to choose who leaves the crew. The two-year AGI picture alarms her, because she can't see herself retraining and has only three months saved. More warning time eases her worry mainly by giving her time to pay down the mortgage and see her children grow up.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she thinks she'd be out of work within two years with nothing lined up and a mortgage still to pay.
whatWouldHelp: Redundancy pay that covers the mortgage, a rule that companies need a union deal before swapping people for robots, and a year of help with the mortgage.
